extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners responsible for internal/employee communication and member-relations programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing, evaluating, and managing employee/member internal-communication programs (models, objectives, media, flows) tailored to organizational structure and environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize purpose over technique in employee publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal employee communications often 'seem to be concerned with format, style, graphics, art work and layout, meeting deadlines, and filling space, more so than with fulfilling a publication’s purpose and objectives.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid producing a 'degree of journalistic slick which does little in communicating to employees but does much to satisfy the ego of the communications technicians.' Focus editorial effort on why an item is in the publication, its purpose and objectives, and its relevance to employees rather than only critiquing layout, pictures, and headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt two-way symmetric internal relations when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs should move toward a 'two-way symmetric model of internal relations' (the 'open organization') that is employee-centered rather than management-centered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use research, solicit employee input, publish employee questions and management answers, and design communications to genuinely help employees evaluate the organization. Two-way symmetric programs incorporate feedback loops and seek mutual understanding rather than one-directional persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet core employee expectations about management and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees want management to: inform them ahead of time about changes affecting jobs; care about how employees feel; give supervisors authority; commit to serving the customer; solve major company problems; run a socially responsible organization; provide new products/services; emphasize quality over quantity; and communicate openly about what it is doing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal-communication programs should provide timely information about changes, demonstrate genuine managerial caring, and communicate management's problem-solving and responsibility. Failure to meet these expectations undermines trust and satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple, accessible media and inquiry mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Symmetric programs use nontraditional, nonprint media and techniques (e.g., IBM's Speak-Up double postcard, employee inquiry features, direct Q&A published for broad interest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide simple, low-friction channels for employees to ask questions (postcards, forms, designated staff to route questions), publish broadly relevant Q&A, and reply directly to individual inquiries when appropriate. Integrate print, video, bulletin-board, and other media to match employee needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize dialogue and interpersonal communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Symmetric programs emphasize interpersonal communication and dialogue with management: briefings, seminars, closed-circuit television, videotape, and interpersonal-communication training for managers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement face-to-face sessions (e.g., breakfasts with executives, small open meetings by department), videotape forums with discussion leaders, telephone-question systems (dial-the-boss), and other interactive formats. Follow up sessions with summaries and action plans for wider staff distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set internal-communication objectives according to organizational goals: control vs. adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal-communication objectives should follow the two general organizational goals: control (typical of more-structured organizations) and adaptation/coordination (typical of less-structured organizations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an organization is highly structured, objectives may emphasize controlling behavior and reinforcing management line; if less structured, objectives should emphasize coordination, information sharing, and facilitating adaptation to the environment. Choose objectives consistent with organizational structure and environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use employee satisfaction as an internal-communication objective where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers identify employee satisfaction with job, supervisor, and the total organization as a major effect of internal communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design communications (content, channels, interpersonal programs) to improve employee perceptions and feelings about work and management, but recognize communication alone may be insufficient without structural or job-design changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use employee performance as an internal-communication objective where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Employee performance (productivity, output, absenteeism, work performance, turnover) is a common objective tied to communication aimed at control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target messages and channels to support job performance (task information, expectations, feedback) while understanding that communication may only sometimes affect performance and often must be complemented by organizational changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: When coordination is the goal, prioritize communication, retention, and acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: For a coordination (symmetric) goal, the relevant communication objectives are 'communication,' 'retention of the message,' and 'acceptance of the message.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate internal programs on whether they get the right information to the right people, whether recipients retain it, and whether they accept/understand it for coordinated collective action among specialists and subsystems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitate inter-subsystem communication to coordinate organizational behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal communication managers in unstructured organizations should 'facilitate symmetric communication between subsystems to coordinate their behavior toward a collective organizational effort.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively create channels, forums, summaries, and mediation roles that help different departments share relevant information (not just through vertical chains). The key is ensuring the correct people get the correct information (amount and quality) at the correct time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor internal-communication systems by contingency (structure + environment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the appropriate goals and communication system after analyzing the organization's structure and environment—no single system fits all organizations or subsystems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use more centralized/formalized downward communication in static environments/subsystems and open symmetric systems with more horizontal/crisscross flows in dynamic environments/subsystems. Analyze each subsystem separately and design communications accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design communications consistent with machine theory where applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: In 'machine theory' organizations communication is asymmetric, emphasizing downward commands, written messages supplemented by oral communication, standardization of roles, unity of command, limited span of control, and discouragement of horizontal grapevine communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the organizational environment and management approach fit machine theory, design communications that reinforce commands, procedures, and rules—use formal written directives and controlled upward channels for critical feedback only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design communications consistent with human relations theory where applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Human relations management emphasizes 'expressive' communication to make workers feel valued (warm 'maple syrup' publications) and uses upward-communication gimmicks (suggestion boxes, open-door policies, picnics) to encourage superficial upward flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expressive messages and symbolic activities to foster morale, but be aware these may be pseudo-involvement if decision-making remains centralized. Evaluate whether such tactics genuinely affect cooperation or only create surface-level goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design communications consistent with human resources theory where applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Human resources theory advocates actual involvement, autonomy, and open symmetric communication (give-and-take between superiors and subordinates), suited for less-structured organizations and professional/specialized employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage participative decision-making, horizontal communication among specialists, and crisscross communication across levels. Provide channels that support genuine employee involvement rather than token feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply systems theory: no all-or-none solution; match system to subsystem needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems theory asserts that 'no one structure—and its accompanying communication system—will be appropriate for all organizations' and that different subsystems may require different communication approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess each system/subsystem's environment and technology; static subsystems will need centralized formal communication emphasizing control, while dynamic subsystems need open symmetric systems emphasizing timely, accurate information flow for coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align internal communication with external-communication objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal communication programs are 'extremely important' because employees are 'a primary source of information for external publics'; failing internal objectives can hinder external objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure employees are informed and accurate messengers for external audiences. Internal programs should support the organization's external image and information needs (e.g., train and inform employees on what to communicate to outsiders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use two-way symmetric communication for associations/member relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Associations (made up of autonomous organizations or individuals) are typically less-structured and their member-communication programs 'must consist of two-way symmetric communication' to provide appropriate information and facilitate member-to-member communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design member communications to deliver essential information when needed and to facilitate interaction among members, recognizing members can join or leave and must be served by timely, relevant two-way channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment internal publics and tailor communication strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees are not a homogeneous public: they work on different tasks, face different problems, and have different autonomy levels; each employee public requires a different communication strategy (Grunig's situational theory adapted to internal publics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify internal publics by task, problem recognition, and autonomy; create targeted messages and channels for each group so they receive information relevant to the problems they face and at the level of autonomy they possess.
